turn_text: Joining us now from, I believe the Capitol is Minnesota's Senator Tina Smith. Senator, thank you so much for joining us today.

Well, good morning, Jeff. Yes, I am here in Washington, D.C., though I'll be heading back to Minnesota. But what it sounds like in the middle of the snow storm this afternoon, so we're looking forward to getting home.

Well, the good news, at least for us here in southern Minnesota, is they've downgraded that chance of snow from like, you know, five to 11 inches down to about three to seven now. So I think as Minnesota is getting towards the end of the winter, we can handle that.

Well, we're talking with you today because of a, you're proposing a bill, you have a bill on the mental health workforce that you've been working on, and we've invited you on to talk about that. Tell us about this bill.

Well, sure. Well, I start from the basic place that mental health care is health care, and yet there are still a lot of challenges for people to get access to the health care that they need, the mental health care that they need, and there's still You know, that's the honest, there's still some stigma around accessing mental health care. And, you know, I want to point out that we've made real progress. And in some of the legislation that we passed last year in Congress is resulting in millions of dollars coming to Minnesota to support better mental health care for school-based services, including in Rochester and other places. So we're making headway, but we still have a real gap because we don't have enough mental health care providers especially in rural communities in small towns. So that's what my bill gets at. I'm excited about it. It's a bipartisan bill and it would provide loan forgiveness for student loan forgiveness for folks that want to go into the mental health field, especially to work in places where there is a shortage of providers.
